title: A genome-wide meta-analysis identifies a sex-specific genetic effect for platelet aggregation in response to agonists.
authors: Nhlbi Trans-Omics For Precision TOPMed Consortium
abstract: Sex-specific genetic effects on platelet aggregation may contribute to differences in thrombotic risk between women and men, yet the underlying genetic mechanisms remain poorly defined. We performed whole-genome sequencing-based genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of 19 harmonized platelet aggregation phenotypes in response to adenosine diphosphate (ADP), epinephrine (EPI), and collagen across three independent cohorts: GeneSTAR, the Framingham Heart Study (FHS) and the Old Order Amish (AMISH). Our meta-GWAS identified a cluster of low-frequency variants within a 20 kb region on chromosome 10 showing strong sex-specific associations with platelet aggregation in response to low-dose EPI. The lead variant, rs116725046, exhibited a genome-wide significant sex interaction (p = 6.7 × 10-9), with opposite phenotypic effects in women and men. Female carriers demonstrated increased platelet aggregation, whereas male carriers showed decreased aggregation, consistent across cohorts. Several variants in tight linkage disequilibrium with the lead variant yielded additional significant interaction signals for low-dose EPI. The associated variants reside within an intronic region of the long noncoding gene LINC00702, with FUMA annotations indicating regulatory chromatin states. Megakaryocyte epigenome data also indicates potential regulatory activity in platelet precursor cells in this genomic region. eQTL analyses suggested sex-differentiated genetic regulation of LINC00702 in multiple tissues, with reduced expression in male heterozygotes only. An Androgen Response Element motif was identified upstream of LINC00702, supporting a potential hormone-responsive regulatory mechanism. Together, these findings identify a novel sex-specific regulatory locus associated with platelet reactivity and highlight LINC00702 as a biologically plausible mediator of sexually dimorphic platelet responses.

title: NiFe (Oxy)hydroxide-Incorporated BiVO4 for Sensitive Photoelectrochemical Detection of Catecholamine.
journal: Langmuir : the ACS journal of surfaces and colloids
abstract: The photoelectrochemical (PEC) detection of catecholamine neurotransmitters has been receiving great attention recently owing to the low cost, fast response, and easy operation. However, the conventional photoactive materials always have relatively low PEC activity, and the PEC signals are prone to interference from the inherent redox reactions at the photoelectrode. Herein, by incorporating the NiFeOOH cocatalyst at the BiVO4 photoelectrode (BiVO4/NiFeOOH), a much higher water oxidation photocurrent was obtained, due to the facilitated hole transport and rapid water oxidation kinetics at the modified ultrathin NiFeOOH layers. Photo-scanning electrochemical microscopy (photo-SECM) was further conducted to reveal the topography and PEC activity of the BiVO4/NiFeOOH, and the local O2 generation rate was inferred by fitting the experimental results. Besides increasing PEC activity, the incorporated NiFeOOH layers would also allow chelating coordination interactions with the catecholamine molecules to achieve sensitive PEC detection. The proposed method would not only offer a new PEC sensing approach for catecholamine detection but also be further expanded to detect other analytes of interest in the biological and environmental fields.

title: Effects of age and education on social cognition: Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test and Mini-SEA.
journal: Archives of clinical neuropsychology : the official journal of the National Academy of Neuropsychologists
abstract: Social cognition is a multidimensional construct encompassing processes such as emotion recognition, theory of mind, and social reasoning. These domains may be differentially affected by aging and educational level. To examine age- and education-related differences in performance on the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET), Facial Emotion Recognition Test (FERT), and Faux Pas Test in cognitively unimpaired young and older adults. A total of 178 cognitively unimpaired participants were included and compared across 3 age groups (17-26, 60-69, and 70-79 years) and 3 education groups (4-8, 9-11, and ≥12 years). Complementary hierarchical regressions examined age and education as continuous variables, with sex, global cognition, depression, and anxiety entered in successive steps. Older age was associated with lower RMET, FERT, and Faux Pas scores. Education was positively associated with RMET performance, negatively associated with FERT performance, and was not independently associated with the Faux Pas total score in the continuous models. Sex was associated only with FERT performance. Adding global cognition, depression, and anxiety did not significantly improve model fit. Age and education were associated with social cognition performance, but the pattern varied by task. These findings support consideration of demographic characteristics when interpreting RMET, FERT, and Faux Pas scores.

title: A Computational Framework for the Determination of the Binding Affinity of Peripheral Proteins to Homogeneous Membranes.
journal: Journal of chemical theory and computation
abstract: Peripheral membrane-binding proteins (PMPs) are essential to immunological and neurological processes, and disruptions in their membrane interactions are implicated in cancer, neurodegeneration, and autoimmune diseases. Their functional diversity arises from the wide range of mechanisms by which they associate with lipid surfaces, motivating atomistic computational frameworks capable of quantifying binding energetics. We present such a methodology and demonstrate it using Bacillus thuringiensis phosphatidylinositol-specific phospholipase C (BtPI-PLC), a 296-residue virulence factor that preferentially associates with phosphatidylcholine (PC) membranes. Experimental studies report dissociation constants near 24 μM for wild-type BtPI-PLC binding to PC vesicles, corresponding to a standard free energy of -6.6 kcal/mol. BtPI-PLC associates with membranes through cation-π interactions involving Y88 and Y246, hydrophobic contacts from helix B, and other noncovalent interactions, making comprehensive sampling challenging. Here, we present a statistical mechanical geometrical route formulation based on the potential of mean force for the quantitative characterization of dilute PMP binding to homogeneous membranes. Using enhanced sampling via well-tempered metadynamics and extended adaptive biasing force, we obtain a computational estimate of the standard binding free energy, -6.2 ± 0.3 kcal/mol, consistent with experimental estimates for BtPI-PLC membrane association.

title: Endothelial Nitric Oxide Synthase Contributes to Recovery Responses Across the Bone Marrow and Kidney Following Acute Exercise.
journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology
abstract: Consistent physical activity reduces chronic disease risk, yet the signaling networks coordinating systemic adaptation remain incompletely defined. Bone marrow (BM) remains understudied as an exercise-responsive tissue despite its roles in hematopoiesis and immune regulation. Being highly vascularized, the BM is positioned to sense metabolic, inflammatory, and hypoxic perturbations during recovery from exercise. Nitric oxide (NO) produced by endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) is rapidly induced by mechanical, metabolic, and hypoxic stimuli and may integrate these signals. We examined recovery-phase responses across BM, kidney oxygen-sensing pathways, and circulating erythropoietin (EPO) to determine the contribution of eNOS to inter-organ recovery responses. In male wild-type (WT) mice, acute exercise induced BM transcriptional programs associated with iron homeostasis, extracellular matrix remodeling, and inflammatory-metabolic signaling. In contrast, eNOS deficiency produced a distinct exercise-responsive transcriptional profile and attenuated exercise-induced EPO and kidney oxygen-sensing responses. Together, these findings identify BM as an exercise-responsive organ during recovery and support an eNOS-dependent coordination between kidney oxygen-sensing, EPO production, and BM transcriptional responses.

title: Patient-reported outcomes after orthopaedic surgery: Addressing non-response, missing data and selection bias.
journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
abstract: Patient-reported outcome measures inform evaluation after orthopaedic surgery, but favourable scores among responders may not reflect outcomes across the entire treated cohort. Non-response, meaning failure to provide requested outcome data, can affect estimates of improvement, procedure comparisons and registry benchmarking. Drawing on examples from anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and knee arthroplasty, this editorial distinguishes missing item responses, missing assessments and incomplete baseline-follow-up pairs. Neither response rates, observed similarities nor statistical adjustments guarantee the absence of non-response bias. Priorities include reporting assessment-specific and paired-analysis denominators, comparing available characteristics of responders and non-responders, documenting reasons for missingness and explaining analytical assumptions. Sensitivity analyses should examine whether clinically plausible assumptions about missing outcomes alter or limit clinical conclusions; reassurance is limited to the scenarios examined. Accessible collection methods and proportionate questionnaire burden may support participation. Conclusions should reflect the population represented, analytical assumptions and remaining uncertainty about the wider treated cohort.

title: Simultaneous Two-Photon Calcium Imaging, Electroencephalography, and Electromyography with Intracortical Electrical Stimulation in Freely Moving Mice.
abstract: Simultaneously combining cellular-resolution imaging, electrical neuromodulation, and electrophysiological monitoring in freely moving mice requires a mechanically stable chronic implant and precise synchronization across recording systems. This protocol describes an integrated preparation for cortical two-photon calcium imaging, intracortical electrical stimulation, electroencephalography (EEG), and electromyography (EMG) in freely moving, tethered mice. Using the retrosplenial cortex as an example target, the protocol details fabrication and implantation of the cranial window and electrodes, viral delivery, optical field localization, installation of a detachable imaging interface, behavioral habituation, multimodal data acquisition, and stimulation-aligned calcium-signal analysis. The preparation permits repeated optical access over short- and long-term intervals and generates cellular-resolution calcium signals together with concurrent electrophysiological and motor-state measurements. Representative outputs include continuous multimodal session-level recordings, mouse-level population calcium responses, and paired stimulation-off and stimulation-on response measures. The workflow can be adapted to other experimentally accessible cortical targets by modifying the cranial-window location, viral injection coordinates, electrode trajectory, and implant geometry.

title: Changes in Histopathology Workload and Diagnostic Patterns During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Retrospective Comparative Study of 2019 and 2020 Records.
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted routine healthcare delivery, including diagnostic and pathology services, potentially affecting specimen submission, laboratory workload, and reporting patterns. Retrospective review of histopathology records can provide a structured approach for evaluating such changes over time. The goal of this protocol was to establish a reproducible method for comparing institutional histopathology records across defined periods and to apply it to the pre-pandemic year 2019 and the COVID-19 pandemic year 2020. Routinely recorded histopathology reports were retrospectively analyzed for annual workload, patient demographics, hospital source, specimen-site distribution, diagnostic categories, malignancy frequency, monthly distribution, and reporting turnaround time. A total of 1,617 records were included, comprising 1,168 from 2019 and 449 from 2020, representing a 61.6% reduction in annual workload. Age and sex distributions were statistically comparable between years, whereas significant differences were observed in hospital source, specimen-site distribution, and diagnostic categories. Monthly distributions were summarized descriptively because valid date coverage was not comparable across the two study years. Gastrointestinal specimens were the most frequent overall, while gynecologic/female genital tract specimens formed a greater proportion of the 2020 workload. Malignant diagnoses decreased from 40 in 2019 to 17 in 2020, although the proportional frequency of malignancy did not differ significantly between years. Among records with valid date information, median reporting turnaround time decreased from 11 days in 2019 to 7 days in 2020. These findings document differences in histopathology service activity between the two periods but do not establish the causes of these changes or the effects of specific operational interventions.

title: Integration of GWAS and Transcriptomic Data Links RMI1, ARHGEF15, TTC21B, and HAGH to Mitochondrial-Neuroinflammatory Coupling in Epilepsy.
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identify epilepsy risk loci but often do not resolve the relevant regulatory genes, cell types, or disease-associated molecular programs. Subtype-resolved genetic evidence was integrated We therefore integrated subtype-resolved epilepsy GWASwith brain expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL), pathology-matched bulk transcriptomics, donor-aware single-cell data, and network analyses to prioritize susceptibility genes and metabolic-immune interaction axes. Summary statistics from eight epilepsy phenotypes underwent quality control, locus definition, SuSiE fine-mapping, brain eQTL colocalization, SMR-HEIDI analysis, and transcriptome-wide association testing. Genetically prioritized genes were evaluated in 162 bulk RNA-seq samples from four epilepsy pathologies and anatomically matched controls. Predefined metabolic and immune modules, cross-pathology coupling, CITE-seq localization in 85,780 cells from six donors, and donor-supported communication were integrated into a source-traceable network according to prespecified decision rules. Integration of 29 fine-mapped phenotype-locus records with colocalization, SMR-HEIDI, and transcriptome-wide association evidence prioritized four Tier 1 genes (RMI1, TVP23B, ARHGEF15, and TTC21B) and four Tier 2 genes (CDK5RAP3, GLS, SUGCT, and HAGH). Six colocalization records were strong, and eight were supportive. Seventeen of 32 gene-pathology results and 64 of 76 module-pathology results met prespecified criteria. Twenty metabolic-immune or gene-module edges and 11 communication interactions were accepted; the strongest coupling linked reduced oxidative phosphorylation with microglial activation (pooled ρ = -0.52) and IL1 signaling (ρ = -0.48). Five genes showed specific cellular localization. The primary network contained 18 nodes and 14 fully traceable edges; three additional relationships were retained only as supplementary contextual links. Convergent genetic, bulk transcriptomic, and single-cell evidence connected the prioritized susceptibility genes to mitochondrial function, glycolysis, lipid handling, neurotransmitter metabolism, microglial activation, cytokine signaling, and vascular or glial states. These findings define genetically anchored hypotheses and candidate pathways for experimental evaluation but do not establish causal direction, molecular interaction, or therapeutic efficacy.

title: Effects of a short-term exercise program on functional capacity and perceived exertion in middle-aged adults: a pilot study.
journal: The Journal of sports medicine and physical fitness
abstract: Physical inactivity is a major modifiable risk factor for chronic diseases and functional decline in adulthood. Although the benefits of exercise are well established, evidence regarding the effectiveness of short-term and easily implementable exercise interventions in real-world settings remains limited. This study aimed to investigate the effects of an 8-week structured physical activity program on functional capacity and perceived exertion in middle-aged adults. Twelve adults aged 50-71 years participated in a quasi-experimental pre-post-intervention study. The intervention consisted of an 8-week supervised exercise program performed 2-3 times per week (45-60 min/session), including aerobic, resistance, mobility, and balance exercises. Functional capacity was assessed before and after the intervention using the Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT), plank test, and Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and paired t-tests. Significant improvements were observed across all outcomes (P<0.05). The distance covered during the 6MWT increased from 459.2±15.4 m to 503.6±15.0 m (+44.4 m; +9.7%), indicating improved functional exercise capacity. Plank performance improved from 35.7±4.0 s to 49.8±4.5 s (+14.2 s; +39.7%), reflecting enhanced core muscular endurance. Perceived exertion decreased from 14.5±0.7 to 11.4±0.5, suggesting improved tolerance to physical activity following the intervention. A short-term and low-complexity exercise program was associated with improvements in functional capacity and reduced perceived exertion in middle-aged adults. These findings support the effectiveness of brief and easily implementable exercise interventions for promoting functional health in real-world settings.

title: Dexmedetomidine attenuates sepsis-induced myocardial injury in association with TRPV1 upregulation and ferroptosis suppression.
abstract: Sepsis-induced myocardial injury involves oxidative stress, iron dysregulation, and ferroptosis-related changes. The role of transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) in mediating the cardioprotective effects of dexmedetomidine (DEX) remains to be elucidated. We evaluated DEX pretreatment in mice subjected to cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) and in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated H9c2 cells, using capsaicin, capsazepine, and ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) as pharmacological probes. A separate 5-day time-course cohort identified day 2 as the peak injury time point based on cardiac injury and biochemical markers, guiding subsequent experiments. In CLP mice, DEX pretreatment improved survival and cardiac function, attenuated myocardial histopathological injury, and reduced oxidative stress and iron accumulation. In H9c2 cells, DEX preserved cell viability and mitochondrial morphology, increased TRPV1, GPX4, and SLC7A11 expression, and decreased ACSL4 expression. Capsaicin reproduced several protective effects of DEX, whereas capsazepine partially attenuated these effects. Fer-1 improved ferroptosis-related indicators and also increased TRPV1 expression. Together, these findings demonstrate consistent DEX-associated protection across animal and cell models, accompanied by TRPV1 upregulation and reduced ferroptosis-related injury. The pharmacological findings support the involvement of TRPV1-sensitive signaling in this protective response.

title: The Primary Cilium: A Small but Powerful Role in Nociceptors.
journal: The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
abstract: Primary cilia are single, microtubule-centered organelles implicated in a variety of key signaling and sensory pathways that contribute to cellular development and tissue homeostasis. Projecting from the basal body of most vertebrate cells, the cilia utilize intraflagellar transport for ciliary trafficking mechanisms that enable Hedgehog, Wnt, and other signal transduction pathways. As a result of mutations in a diverse set of genes, clinical conditions known as "ciliopathies" feature the involvement of multiple organ systems, including the central and peripheral nervous systems. Recent preclinical studies implicate the primary cilium in essential basic processes in nociception such as threshold and sensitization, without a clear and consistent nociceptive phenotype apparent in ciliopathy patients. Investigating the relationship between primary cilia, signaling pathways such as Hedgehog and Wnt, and their roles in nociception may allow new therapeutic options for modulation of chronic pain states.

title: Differential impact of dynein pathogenic variants on mitotic spindle organization and cortical organoid growth.
abstract: Mutations in the dynein heavy chain gene (DYNC1H1) cause a spectrum of neurological disorders, including malformations of cortical development (MCD) and spinal muscular atrophy with lower extremity predominance (SMALED). How these mutations differentially affect dynein functions in the nervous system, leading to distinct pathologies, remains unknown. Using patient-derived cortical organoids, we address how MCD- and SMALED-causing dynein mutations alter human cortical development. We show that MCD-associated mutations alter the growth of organoids, but that SMALED organoids are unaffected, consistent with the microcephaly phenotypes of individuals with MCD. These defects are mirrored by a large increase in apoptotic cell death in MCD organoids. MCD mutations - but not SMALED mutations - strongly affect radial glial progenitor divisions, by inducing severe mitotic spindle defects and leading to prolonged mitotic duration. Mitotic checkpoint inhibition alleviates mitotic delay but fails to prevent apoptosis, indicating that mitotic arrest is not the cause of cell death in MCD. These findings reveal how specific dynein mutations can distinctly disrupt cortical development, establishing mitotic spindle dysfunction and apoptosis as central mechanisms underlying dynein-related microcephaly.

title: Compensatory Trunk Neuromuscular Control During Early Rehabilitation After Motor Incomplete Spinal Cord Injury.
abstract: Motor incomplete spinal cord injury (SCI) reduces trunk control and limits function of the limbs, yet mechanisms underlying trunk neuromuscular recovery remain unclear. This observational study investigated changes in trunk motor control in individuals with recent motor incomplete cervical or thoracic SCI. Thirty-six participants with SCI and 20 controls were recruited from hospitals and the community, respectively. All participants with SCI received tailored inpatient rehabilitation and were assessed at baseline and 4 weeks later. Participants performed trunk goal-directed tasks: forward and lateral reaches, and postural tasks: bilateral shoulder flexion at comfortable and rapid speeds, while we recorded lumbar erector spinae (ES) muscle activity using high-density surface electromyography (HDsEMG) and trunk and upper-limb movement with 2D video. The American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale (AIS) total motor scores were also collected. Lumbar ES EMG activity was lower in participants with SCI than in controls. In SCI, ES activation was more caudal during shoulder flexion than forward reaching, while controls showed consistent patterns across tasks. After 4 weeks of rehabilitation, participants with SCI significantly improved motor scores, forward reaching distance, and trunk displacement. Participants with AIS C exhibited a progressive caudal shift in ES activation over time, while those with AIS D showed a stable activation pattern. These findings indicate that improvements in trunk function after SCI may arise through different neuromuscular strategies depending on injury severity. Incorporating additional trunk-focused kinematics and HDsEMG measurements may help to detect these compensatory patterns early, guiding interventions that balance compensation with strategies that promote more optimal trunk control.

title: Evidence appraisal of clinical practice guidelines for managing menopausal symptoms: a systematic literature review.
abstract: Symptoms associated with menopause can significantly impair quality of life. Although menopausal hormone therapy remains a well-established and highly effective intervention, a wide range of nonhormone therapies are available on and off-label as options for women in whom menopausal hormone therapy is contraindicated or not preferred. Although multiple clinical guidelines address the use of menopausal hormone therapy and nonhormone therapy for managing symptoms of menopause, the consistency of the recommendations and the robustness of the supporting evidence remain uncertain. Evaluate current United States menopause treatment guidelines in the context of emerging therapies (menopausal hormone therapy and nonhormone therapy) and evolving clinical practice. We systematically searched PubMed and EMBASE for United States menopause treatment guidelines published between 2014 and 2024. We included clinical practice guidelines and consensus statements, excluding those limited to surgically induced menopause. We extracted data using the Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes, Recommendation framework and assessed guideline quality. Of 655 records screened, 13 met the inclusion criteria from organizations including the American Association of Clinical Endocrinology, The Menopause Society, and the Endocrine Society. Guidelines evaluated menopausal hormone therapy for managing vasomotor symptoms, genitourinary syndrome, premature ovarian insufficiency, hypoactive sexual desire disorder, sleep disturbances, and depression, contingent on individual risk profiles. Nonhormone therapies, including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, gabapentin, and fezolinetant, were supported by moderate to high-quality evidence. Most guidelines advise against over-the-counter or alternative treatments due to limited data. No guideline provided decision-support tools or therapeutic sequencing algorithms for nonhormone therapy selection. Seven guidelines were of moderate quality, four low-moderate, and two low quality with none rated high quality, primarily due to gaps in stakeholder involvement and applicability. This review highlights variable quality and consistency in United States clinical recommendations for vasomotor symptoms. Future guidelines should incorporate structured decision frameworks to guide therapy selection based on contraindications, patient preferences, and risk profiles.

title: Comparative Binding Profiles of Co-Crystallized Ligands at Human Phosphodiesterase 1B Using Molecular Dynamics Simulations and Binding Free Energy Analysis.
abstract: Phosphodiesterases (PDEs) biochemically break down cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) and cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), which functionally regulate cyclic nucleotide signaling pathways. cAMP/cGMP signaling has been associated with neurodegenerative disorders like Alzheimer's disease (AD). The present in silico study focuses on the three co-crystallized ligands 0NY, 8HM, and 8HP bound to phosphodiesterase 1B (PDE1B), assessing structural stability via root mean square deviation (RMSD), conformational dynamics via root mean square fluctuation (RMSF), and hydrogen bonding and binding energetics by molecular mechanics-generalized Born surface area (MM-GBSA) calculations. All molecular complexes stayed stable across the 300 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, with RMSF calculations indicating local flexibility in recognition loops while maintaining overall structural stability. Further, the complexes had stable radius of gyration (Rg) profiles. Nonetheless, the 8HM-PDE1B complex was the most stable and showed the lowest backbone and atomic fluctuation. Principal component analysis (PCA) illustrated that the 8HM-PDE1B complex was stable, while the 8HP-PDE1B and 0NY-PDE1B complexes elicited comparatively broader conformational states. The high binding affinity of 8HM for PDE1B (-49.93 kcal/mol) was driven by van der Waals and electrostatic forces, with the binding energy decomposition assessment identifying residues I371, L388, Q421, and F424 with vital roles in ligand interactions. Conclusively, amongst the three compounds investigated, 8HM emerged as the strongest and most stable PDE1B ligand.

title: Applying functional MRI analysis techniques to whole-brain calcium-imaging data to investigate structural and functional relationships in Drosophila melanogaster.
abstract: Clarifying the relationship between structure and function is important for understanding the brain. In Drosophila melanogaster, FlyEM and FlyWire electron microscopy-based connectome data, and whole-brain calcium-imaging data are available. We applied pre-processing methods from functional magnetic resonance imaging to whole-brain calcium-imaging data and comprehensively investigated the optimal parameters. Then, we found that the FC-SC (functional and structural connectivity) correlation decreased linearly with region of interest count, and this trend was the same in flies and humans. We also developed a new, more robust method to quantify the degree of pre- and post-synaptic segregation, and investigated this in the fly whole-brain. This revealed that many neurons have unsegregated synapses. We extracted highly unsegregated synapses and compared them with random-extracted null SC matrices. Their FC-SC correlation was significantly higher, indicating that these synapses contribute to FC well. Conversely, highly segregated synapses showed significantly lower FC-SC correlation and contribute less to FC. Neurons with unsegregated synapses, like non-spiking neurons, are spread throughout the whole-brain, and they are thought to have a significant influence on FC.

title: The Sleep-Aging-Motor Memory Triad: A Systematic Review of Task-Dependent Consolidation and Neuroplasticity.
abstract: Motor learning includes a set of processes linked to practice and experience that are crucial for gaining new skills and altering behavior as time progresses. Proficiency in motor skills is crucial for maintaining autonomy and enhancing quality of life in older adults. Nonetheless, recent findings indicate that age-related sleep alterations significantly impair motor memory consolidation, thus speeding up the decline of motor abilities. Within this context, motor learning depends not only on internal neural processes but also on sleep quality, especially the preservation of slow-wave and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Disruptions to these sleep stages may interfere with the neural processes necessary for the long-term consolidation of motor skills. This synthesis emphasizes the importance of recognizing the relationship among sleep, aging, and sensorimotor plasticity, while suggesting effective intervention strategies like improving sleep or specific therapies to alleviate age-related motor deficits. These findings originate from a pre-registered systematic review of 26 research articles extracted from 740 sources indexed in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. We investigated these effects on motor learning and whether they vary by task type, complexity, sleep effect, and age. This review seeks to enhance our comprehension of age-suitable empirical studies on sleep-related motor memory consolidation among healthy groups by synthesizing results from various research projects.

title: Accuracy and Difficulty of the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test Across Racial Groups.
abstract: Prior research has identified racial group differences in performance on social cognitive tasks related to emotion recognition. Little work has examined racial group differences within the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET), a task designed to assess theory of mind, particularly among American samples. Further, our understanding of participants' perceived ease of the task and its association with performance on social cognition tasks is lacking. This study sought to fill this gap using two university samples. In sample 1, undergraduates (n = 1,494) provided data including the RMET and demographic information. In sample 2, undergraduates (n = 189) completed the RMET with additional questions assessing perceived ease of RMET items, as well as demographic information. Participants identifying as White, Asian, or an other race performed significantly better on the RMET than Black participants. No significant differences were found between racial minority and White participants on perceived ease of the RMET. Race did not significantly moderate associations between perceived ease and performance. This study adds to the growing body of evidence suggesting that diverse samples may exhibit racial differences in performance on the RMET. Additional work should clarify whether discrepancies in perceived and objective social cognition performance vary by racial groups.

title: AI-Driven Intelligent ECM-Mimetic Hydrogel Scaffolds for Brain Organoid Engineering.
abstract: Brain organoids are increasingly used for scalable modeling of human neurodevelopment and disease, but their reproducibility and translational value remain limited by reliance on ill-defined matrices such as Matrigel. Although Matrigel provides several brain-relevant features, including soft, viscoelastic, and non-fibrillar properties, its composition is poorly defined, batch-variable, and difficult to tune in a standardized manner. Considering the physicochemical characteristics of the native brain extracellular matrix (ECM), brain organoid culture requires ECM-like materials that reproduce brain-specific mechanical, transport, and signaling cues rather than merely providing 3D support. This review presents a rational framework for engineering intelligent ECM-mimetic hydrogel scaffolds for advanced brain organoid culture. It summarizes key features of the native brain ECM and introduces material rationality as the systematic selection and engineering of hydrogels according to brain-specific biological, physical, and translational design requirements. The review also highlights how artificial intelligence (AI) can navigate high-dimensional material design spaces through surrogate modeling, digital twins, and closed-loop optimization informed by multi-physics and multi-omics feedback. Ultimately, AI-driven scaffold design may enable more reproducible, mature, and scalable brain organoid models.

title: The adverse skeletal and reproductive impact of the 5:2 diet in mice.
abstract: Despite being a popular weight-loss strategy, a rigorous understanding of the broader physiological consequences of the 5:2 diet remains surprisingly poor. Since we have previously shown that the metabolic effects of the 5:2 diet in mice are both sex- and ghrelin-dependent, we have now explored the impact of this diet on indices of skeletal and reproductive function. Adolescent male and female wild-type (WT) and loxTB-GHSR (GHSR-null) mice were ad libitum-fed or maintained on the 5:2-diet for 3 or 6 weeks with skeletal and reproductive function assessed in terminal samples. The 5:2 diet only reduced weight gain in male WT mice. Although the 5:2 diet had little impact on longitudinal skeletal growth, the mid-diaphyseal femoral cortex showed lateral wall thickening and medial wall thinning, coupled with indices of slower trabecular remodelling. While the 5:2 diet had no significant impact on indices of reproductive axis function in females, male mice maintained on the 5:2 diet for 3 weeks demonstrated declining gonadotropin secretion without concomitant reductions in either spermatogenesis or steroidogenesis. However, by 6 weeks, circulating testosterone in 5:2-fed males had declined by 96%. Loss of GHSR, the receptor for ghrelin, had a similar impact. The popularity of the 5:2 diet as a weight loss strategy disguises its physiological impact. When coupled with our previous evidence that the 5:2 diet enhances lipid storage, our current results indicate that infradian stimulation of the ghrelin axis by the 5:2 diet is accompanied by some undesirable endocrine consequences, particularly in males.

title: Neurovascular Unit and Brain Microenvironment Research in Cerebral Small Vessel Disease: A Bibliometric Analysis.
abstract: Cerebral small vessel disease is commonly identified using magnetic resonance imaging markers, but increasing attention has been paid to the neurovascular unit and the brain microenvironment. This study aims to characterize the structure of a search-defined, neurovascular-topic-conditioned CSVD bibliometric literature; not to discover mechanisms or infer their causal order. We performed a bibliometric and visual analysis using a Web of Science Core Collection primary dataset, a focused Web of Science Core Collection dataset constructed with specific neurovascular unit and brain microenvironment terms, and a complementary PubMed/ MEDLINE dataset with human-related filters. VOSviewer, CiteSpace, Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny, and Microsoft Excel were used to analyze publication output, collaboration patterns, co-cited references, keyword co-occurrence, thematic evolution, and thematic patterns across datasets. The historical primary WoSCC export comprised 2,325 records and the historical focused export 1,118 records. An independently retrieved 368-PMID index-filtered subset provided title-based thematic description. The network and burst figures describe these frozen historical exports, while separate, later sensitivity checks assess dependence on retrieval and indexing. The five prespecified domains represent the literature targeted by the searches rather than independent thematic discoveries. Search-term conditioning, indexing status, database coverage, heterogeneous disease constructs, and network settings constrain the interpretation of mapped patterns. This bibliometric study describes selected neurovascular and microenvironment-related CSVD research, without demonstrating causal mechanisms, unbiased field-wide thematic emergence, or validated clinical targets.

title: Ergothioneine in Neuroprotection and Cognitive Function: Implications for Brain Disorders.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterised by progressive neuronal loss and continue to be significant health issues worldwide. Oxidative stress is a central and unifying pathway that mediates neurodegeneration by interacting with neuroinflammation, mitochondrial pathophysiology, protein aggregation, excitotoxicity, and neurovascular dysfunction. Existing treatments are mostly symptomatic and do not effectively target the upstream pathological events. Therefore, there is an urgent need for new neuroprotective agents that are more effective and specific for treating these conditions. Ergothioneine (ET), a sulfur-containing amino acid obtained from dietary sources, is a promising neuroprotective candidate because of its distinctive biochemical and pharmacokinetic properties. ET shows unmatched stability and antioxidant behaviour, undergoes selective cellular uptake via OCTN1/SLC22A4, and has been detected in brain tissue in experimental models; however, the extent and mechanism of its delivery across the intact blood-brain barrier, particularly in humans, remain incompletely established. ET has demonstrated multi-targeted neuroprotective potential in preclinical models, including direct scavenging of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, modulation of endogenous antioxidant systems, metal-ion chelation, preservation of mitochondrial function, regulation of inflammatory responses, and modulation of apoptotic pathways. ET improved cognitive performance and restored redox homeostasis in experimental animal models. Although encouraging, clinical evidence remains limited. To demonstrate the efficacy of ET as a therapeutic and preventive measure for neurodegenerative diseases, future studies should use large-scale clinical trials, dose optimisation, and biomarker-based strategies. Furthermore, ET exhibits several pharmacokinetic and biochemical properties of potential relevance to neuroprotection, including OCTN1- mediated cellular uptake, prolonged tissue retention, and antioxidant activity. Although ET has been detected in brain tissue in experimental models, its transport across the intact blood-brain barrier and the extent of brain exposure in humans remain incompletely established.
